limitations: This is not a ban on every boolean parameter or boolean data. Optional, nullable, literal-only, generic, destructured, indirect-predicate and changed-binding inputs remain outside the owned direct broad-boolean check.
Arbitrary multi-statement bodies, leading directives, short-circuit guards, local predicate aliases and arbitrary flow are not inferred. A call may be pure; a warning remains manual design guidance.

The native block-body detector retains its on[A-Z] object-property exemption. The concise-arrow extension does not infer a callback contract from that name. This known false negative remains documented rather than hidden in precision claims.

Noncomputed property reads count as syntactic data without proving getter effects. Computed reads, including literal keys, remain outside that exemption and can still warn in block mappings. No universal getter or function purity proof is claimed.

Immutable identifier aliases are bounded; mutated bindings are not flow-tracked. A function used as a callback and direct operation may retain the independent callback signature without proving all API design optimal.

Member callback-reference analysis is conservative. Property replacement, dynamic access, escaping receivers and arbitrary aliases can prevent or weaken proof; no whole-program ownership guarantee is claimed.

Same-operation data selection requires a stable resolved callable/simple target and selected data within the documented syntax boundary. Matching text or familiar formatting-function names alone is insufficient.

No-return-assign preserves individual grouping and common memoization, but formatters may change advisory coverage and native chained assignments may produce repeated-span reports. Update/delete and other returned mutations are outside its assignment-specific scope.

Ruff FBT remains syntax-oriented: Annotated/literal/alias spellings and lambda defaults have documented gaps; protocol/abstract/overload declarations are not blanket exempt. Existing keyword-only, named-data, allowed-call and compatibility boundaries remain authoritative.
Every new design diagnostic remains warning severity with no intent-changing autofix. Error promotion requires separate warning-release evidence and metadata review.

The owned selector warning uses @sarj/no-boolean-selector-parameter. Existing direct sonarjs/no-selector-parameter suppression comments target the previous rule ID; reasoned exceptions need review against the new owned ID. No consumers or suppression comments were rewritten automatically.

passes.question: Does the maintained detector retain ordinary block if/else dispatch?
passes.decision: Retain maintained S2301 block coverage through one owned warning.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Does the maintained detector retain returned effectful conditionals?
passes.decision: Retain maintained effectful conditional coverage through one owned warning.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { return flag ? a() : b(); }

passes.question: Can concise-arrow syntax hide equivalent operation dispatch?
passes.decision: Add one expression-bodied arrow listener sharing the typed eligibility and contract filters.

example.source: const select = (flag: boolean) => flag ? a() : b();

passes.question: Do parentheses around a concise conditional change dispatch ownership?
passes.decision: Cover the equivalent concise arrow without rewriting AST nodes or parent identities.

example.source: const select = (flag: boolean) => (flag ? a() : b());

passes.question: Does negating the concise-arrow test preserve operation selection?
passes.decision: Cover direct logical negation of the same boolean parameter.

example.source: const select = (flag: boolean) => !flag ? b() : a();

passes.question: Does async concise-arrow dispatch need the same warning boundary?
passes.decision: Cover effectful async concise conditionals; keep manual remediation.

example.source: const select = async (flag: boolean) => flag ? await a() : await b();

passes.question: Should arbitrary multi-statement functions be inferred as dispatchers?
passes.decision: Defer arbitrary control-flow analysis; multiple responsibilities and surrounding work need separate evidence.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { record(); if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Should a leading directive cause an unsupported control-flow expansion?
passes.decision: Document the leading-directive blind spot; do not synthesize an upstream function body.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { "use strict"; return flag ? a() : b(); }

passes.question: Is direct negated block dispatch already covered?
passes.decision: Retain the direct negated test and unchanged-binding boundary.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { if (!flag) { b(); } else { a(); } }

passes.question: Should boolean-literal comparisons be added to the direct-test scope?
passes.decision: Abstain on comparisons; the owned rule deliberately checks only a direct identifier or its logical negation.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { if (flag === true) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Does an inferred boolean default retain typed selector ownership?
passes.decision: Resolve the inferred broad boolean with the native checker; retain warning coverage.

example.source: function select(flag = false) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Does a boolean type alias retain typed selector ownership?
passes.decision: Resolve aliases by type and binding rather than matching bool annotation spelling.

example.source: type Flag = boolean; function select(flag: Flag) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Should an optional input be treated as a two-state selector?
passes.decision: Abstain on optional three-state contracts rather than infer two-state ownership.

example.source: function select(flag?: boolean) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Should a nullable input be treated as a two-state selector?
passes.decision: Abstain on nullable three-state contracts rather than infer two-state ownership.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean | null) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Does a true-or-false literal union normalize to broad boolean?
passes.decision: Retain normalized broad-boolean ownership.

example.source: function select(flag: true | false) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Should a single boolean literal receive a duplicate design warning?
passes.decision: Abstain on literal-only inputs; constant-condition checks retain their existing ownership.

example.source: function select(flag: true) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Can a generic constrained input be treated as an owned broad boolean?
passes.decision: Abstain on constrained generic inputs; do not derive independent ownership from inference.

example.source: function select<T extends boolean>(flag: T) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Does an independent class method retain selector coverage?
passes.decision: Retain coverage unless the exact member or a proven callback reference establishes a separate contract.

example.source: class Service { select(flag: boolean) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } } }

passes.question: Does generator syntax preserve effectful operation selection?
passes.decision: Retain native generator effect coverage; no API-changing autofix.

example.source: function* select(flag: boolean) { return flag ? yield a() : yield b(); }

passes.question: Is short-circuit optional work proof of alternate-operation dispatch?
passes.decision: Defer guard-only short-circuit work; optional work does not establish alternate operations.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { flag && a(); }

passes.question: Is a guard-return clause proof of alternate-operation dispatch?
passes.decision: Preserve guard clauses; no arbitrary function-size or one-return policy is introduced.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { if (!flag) return; a(); }

passes.question: Does using a boolean as predicate input make it the direct selector test?
passes.decision: Filter the upstream report when the boolean merely supplies data to another predicate.

example.source: function observe(flag: boolean) { if (validate(flag)) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Do unresolved same-name calls establish one stable operation with selected data?
passes.decision: Keep the warning when format is unresolved. Independently resolved stable same-operation calls with selected data are preserved in the owned regression suite.

example.source: function label(flag: boolean) { return flag ? format("yes") : format("no"); }

passes.question: Should pure if/else value mapping differ from a pure conditional expression?
passes.decision: Preserve syntactically proven pure mappings consistently across equivalent source shapes.

example.source: function label(flag: boolean) { if (flag) { return "yes"; } else { return "no"; } }

passes.question: Does a pure returned conditional remain accepted?
passes.decision: Preserve pure boolean-to-value conversion.

example.source: function label(flag: boolean) { return flag ? "yes" : "no"; }

passes.question: Does a destructured named-options contract remain outside direct parameters?
passes.decision: Retain the structured-options exclusion; named arguments do not prove single responsibility.

example.source: function select({flag}: {flag: boolean}) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } }

passes.question: Does an inline callback preserve its external boolean-input contract?
passes.decision: Preserve direct callback identity, including runtime-erased wrappers.

example.source: events.subscribe((flag: boolean) => { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } });

passes.question: Does an unresolved named subscriber establish an independent boolean callback contract?
passes.decision: Keep the warning when events.subscribe is unresolved. The independently typed preserved counterpart is selector-contract/named-arrow-contract.

example.source: function onState(flag: boolean) { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } } events.subscribe(onState);

passes.question: Is an onX property name alone semantic evidence of a callback contract?
passes.decision: Document the inherited native block-body exemption as a blind spot; concise extension does not adopt the name heuristic.

example.source: const handlers = { onState: (flag: boolean) => { if (flag) { a(); } else { b(); } } };

passes.question: Should local aliases and extra statements trigger inferred dispatch ownership?
passes.decision: Defer local predicate aliases and added statements rather than infer intent from matching names.

example.source: function select(flag: boolean) { const enabled = flag; return enabled ? a() : b(); }

passes.question: Does the selector policy honor the inline arrow contract boundary?
passes.decision: preserve: Direct callback argument independently establishes a boolean-input contract.

example.source:
declare function left(): number; declare function right(): number; declare function subscribe(callback: (value: boolean) => void): void;
subscribe((value: boolean) => { if (value) { left(); } else { right(); } });

passes.question: Does the selector policy honor the inline function contract boundary?
passes.decision: preserve: Direct function-expression callback retains its boolean input.

example.source:
declare function left(): number; declare function right(): number; declare function subscribe(callback: (value: boolean) => void): void;
